A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Speculative Verdict work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, recovery statistics and model-pool experiments in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, critic comparisons, cost measurements and analyses of consensus selection and failures.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same normalized answer-NLL consensus score, cross-all expert selection, reasoning drafts and single verdict synthesis call. The structured image input already appears in v1. Newly tested scoring variants are ablations, without a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four original benchmarks and adds TallyQA-Complex and MathVista (Table 2, Section 4.4). Relational counting and visual mathematical reasoning substantially broaden evaluation beyond the original information-intensive and high-resolution tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds Pixel-Reasoner to benchmark comparisons, o1 to performance/cost comparisons, and LLaVA-Critic-7B/72B with pointwise and pairwise judging. Conversely, the standalone Qwen2.5-VL-72B comparator disappears from the retained alternative-pool comparisons in Tables 12–13, although it remains in the main comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include MathVista-testmini, 1000 sampled TallyQA-Complex questions, and 1000-instance-per-benchmark cost comparisons. Appendix G introduces judging controls with three versus five candidates, pointwise versus pairwise decisions, different judge sizes and an alternative verdict sharing the critic's backbone. Table 4 also expands the small-verdict configurations.

E4.justification: v2 adds normalization and answer-only versus full-trajectory NLL ablations, selection-frequency analysis, expert-complementarity analysis and SV's own failure analysis (Appendices F, I and J). It also expands verdict-scale and judging analyses. The earlier visual-input, structured-input, recovery and DeepEyes analyses are largely retained; alternative-pool experiments no longer report the Qwen72B verdict.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. New frequencies and averages extend descriptive results without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 scores remain unchanged, while v2 adds substantial benchmark, critic, cost and diagnostic results, including SV accuracies of 76.9 on TallyQA-Complex and 82.9 on MathVista. Its verdict-scale table replaces InfographicVQA values, including GLM's 86.0 with 84.7, while dropping v1's 1000-sample qualifier; these are not established same-setting performance changes. The alternative-pool Qwen72B-verdict results of 84.2 and 80.4 disappear. Section 4.2 also corrects the ChartQAPro improvement from 6.6 to 6.7 points.

T1.justification: The NLL, relative consensus and global consensus definitions remain mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2's added calibration and off-policy discussions remain empirical explanations.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free draft/verdict synthesis, consensus selection, error correction and cost efficiency. The introduction's principal contributions also remain unchanged; the additions mainly expand supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting normalization to selection collapse and expert specialization to complementary reasoning. Appendix J newly identifies SV's limitations: fine-grained extraction, color matching and a verdict favoring verbose incorrect drafts despite correct majority evidence. This substantially qualifies v1's emphasis on successful recovery and competing tool pipelines' weaknesses.

D1.justification: v2 documents the critic's evaluation template and pairwise elimination procedure and expands the explanation of answer-only NLL scoring. Section 7 now states that supplementary material includes anonymized source code, while the abstract retains the same public repository link. Existing SV prompts and structured-image preprocessing details remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through new discussions of general VLM reasoning and LMM-as-a-Judge, including LLaVA-Critic and multimodal evaluation research. SV is explicitly situated relative to selection-based judges. The original language-model ensemble discussion is retained in Appendix B rather than removed.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition, including the abstract, method and conclusion, is preserved. Changes include localized results-paragraph rewrites, reorganized related work, the ensemble discussion's move to Appendix B, and revised ethics and reproducibility wording. Much of the expansion is new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial table displays for benchmarks, costs, tokens, normalization, critics, complementarity and failures. Figure 8 gains critic bars, and main and alternative-pool tables gain comparison rows and revised formatting. Existing method, qualitative and prompt graphics are largely retained; the earlier recovery Figure 9 is redisplayed with a Table 11 caption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of consensus and synthesis through normalization ablations, critic comparisons using a shared backbone, and explicit analysis of SV's failures—important gaps in v1's evidence. Additional tasks and comparative costs further improve assessment of applicability and efficiency. Reporting limitations remain: API/token accounting does not establish full-pipeline cost, the verdict-scale subset becomes unclear, and Section 4.5's stated 72B critic gain range does not match Table 20. These issues limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.
